name: Sahaptin, Umatilla dialect
confidence_why: Hargus & Beavert (2006, 2014, 2016) and Jansen (2010) describe Sahaptin accent as morpheme-inherent and unpredictable in the Yakima dialect, Rude (2012) says the same of Sahaptin from Umatilla data, and the only disagreement on record, between Jacobs (1931) and Rude (1988) on whether Umatilla-area words carry extra secondary stresses, is a matter of detail rather than of the lexical type.

catalog_quote: Sahaptin contains many of the classic properties of accentual systems (McCawley 1978): unpredictable location of accent within morphemes, a contrast between accented vs. unaccented morphemes, and a culminativity principle. In addition, high pitch is a phonetic correlate of accent (Hargus and Beavert to appear), as is often the case in such systems. All Sahaptin data in this article come from the second author, who is a native speaker of the Yakima dialect. ... Yakima Sahaptin roots vary in length, with most roots one to three syllables long. In roots, accent (transcribed here with acute accent) can fall on any syllable: [ánut’at] ‘orphan’, [talámat] ‘pipe’, [anahúj] ‘black bear’. ... new_statements.quote: Stress and high tone are one phenomenon in northern Sahaptin; they are very strongly marked in northwest Sahaptin. In the latter group, ordinary words have only one syllable accented and no secondary stress; [...] In the Umatilla reservation dialects there may be two, three or four accented syllables to a word, each accent gentle, with only slightly higher tone; the rules for stress in these dialects are quite elaborate. In all dialects the syllable that has the stress takes high or falling—that is, high to normal—tone. [p.117] ... Wherever morphologic affixes are used, stress is governed rigidly by such grammatical factors. [...] In walu'la-palu·'s, stress is given to all roots and all sorts of morphologic elements that may or may not take word stress in northwest Sahaptin. [p.118]

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for 'Sahaptin, Umatilla dialect' has an empty rule and there are no existing statements, so nothing to agree or disagree with; Jacobs supplies the first sourced description: accent = stress plus high tone, morphologically/lexically governed rather than edge-fixed, and, specifically for the Umatilla reservation dialects (which for him include yumati'la = Umatilla), several gentle accents per word with elaborate, only partly stated rules. Note that his detailed rules are drawn from northwest Sahaptin (Klikitat, Taitnapam) and his Umatilla-reservation verb data are 'at least' walu'la-palu's; Umatilla (yumati'la) notes came from two informants (Allan Pa'tawa, Celestine Mintho…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress and high tone are a single accent in northern Sahaptin (stressed short vowel = high tone, stressed long vowel/diphthong = falling tone). Placement is not tied to a word edge: in affixed words it is dictated by which morphemes are present (certain noun postpositions -pama', -i'k, -(y)a'i etc. and verb affixes a'-, pa'-, -i'k, -a'c.. invariably take the accent; otherwise the root, in verbs usually the first syllable of the root complex), while for affixless adverbs, particles and many nouns 'it seems impossible to determine rules for the presence of stress'; stress distinguishes only the pa-/pa'- homonyms. For the Umatilla reservation dialects (Jacobs's group = yumati'la [Umatilla], walu'la, palu's, p. 96) a word may carry two to four gentle accents with only slightly higher tone and the rules are 'quite elaborate'; in walu'la-palu's every root and many morphological elements are stressed, each verb root of a multi-root verb is stressed unless a penultimate -ca'/-xa'/-ta' or an accented prefix intervenes, and noun-pronoun-adverb accentuation follows the northwest Sahaptin rules (p. 120).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Northwest Sahaptin: explicitly 'no secondary stress' (one accent per word; freshly compounded words may have two equal stresses). Umatilla reservation dialects: two, three or four accented syllables per word, each gentle; coordinate stresses on each root in multi-root verbs (walu'la-palu's), with a suggested drift toward penultimate accent in the walu'la-palu's verb (p. 119).
new_statements.exceptions: Monosyllabic words normally stressed with high tone but the connective ku- is never stressed and behaves as a proclitic; connective a'uku/auku' forms vary in stress and tone; affixless adverbs, particles and many nouns have no determinable rule; -pama' outranks all other accented noun suffixes except possessive -mi', itself superseded by rare final -aipa'x and -xana'tt; anterior root -qala- is almost never accented; palu's alone has final past-tense -ya' accentuation; in walu'la-palu's aspect/tense suffixes take stress when followed by further suffixes or enclitics, and enclitics may be stressed (cala'wica·'c); Jacobs states he has 'not supplied all the rules for verb stress in walu'la-palu's'.
new_statements.identity_note: Jacobs 1931 is a grammar of 'northern Sahaptin' built on northwest Sahaptin notes (Klikitat/xwa'lxwaipam 1926 and upper Cowlitz/ta'idnapam 1927; 'examples in the grammar are of ta'idnapam provenience unless otherwise noted', p. 96). The Umatilla dialect proper (his yumati'la) is covered only as part of his 'Umatilla reservation dialects' group together with walu'la (Walla Walla) and palu's (Palus), which he says 'constitute a dialect intelligible to all the northwest Sahaptins' (p. 96); his Umatilla-reservation stress details are stated for 'walu'la-palu's' or 'the Umatilla reservation bands, or at least walu'la-palu's' (p. 120), with yumati'la notes from Allan Pa'tawa and Celestine Minthorn (p. 98) not separately exemplified. The multiple-accent statement on p. 117 is the one sentence that applies to the Umatilla reservation dialects as a whole.

readall_conflicts: The one listed work could not be opened, so no direct conflict with the catalog (whose rule field for this item is empty) can be established. Among the on-disk Sahaptin sources read for context, there is a documented disagreement about secondary stress, not about primary placement: Jacobs 1931: 117 (as quoted in Hargus & Beavert 2016: 3) says northwest Sahaptin words carry one accented syllable and no secondary stress whereas 'the Umatilla reservation dialects' may have two to four accented syllables per word; Rude 1988 (as quoted in the same place) says the language as a whole has three stress levels with predictable secondary stress in reduplication and in the imperfective/habitual past suffixes; Hargus & Beavert (2016: 3) find no secondary stress in Yakima outside long reduplicated verbs. On primary accent all sources agree it is morpheme-inherent and lexically located (Rude 2006: 271; Rude 2012: 301-302; Hargus & Beavert 2014: 333-334; 2016: 2), with Hargus & Beavert calling the Yakima system a lexical pitch accent ('between stress and tone').
